components.text: Whether divine grounding explains the categories and establishes that the proposed guarantor actually exists.
Whether coherence of categories inside a theistic worldview establishes the truth or necessity of that worldview.
The decisive demand is whether divine grounding demonstrates an existing and specifically adequate guarantor, rather than merely describing a coherent belief.
The comparative claim also requires showing that theism's coherence establishes its truth rather than only compatibility with the categories.
Whether rational reliance on logic requires an absolute external guarantee rather than demonstrated reliability.
Whether use of logical principles commits the user to certainty about their ultimate metaphysical ground.
The decisive component is whether rational reliance on logical laws requires an absolute external guarantee beyond their repeatedly demonstrated reliability.
Whether the categories must have a further foundation and whether positing God resolves rather than relocates that demand.
Whether failure of empirical proof establishes that a transcendent foundation must exist.
The decisive demand is to show that a further foundation is necessary and that defining God as foundational explains rather than relocates the difficulty.
The further claim that logical or inductive assumptions cannot simply be basic also requires demonstration rather than an assertion of explanatory need.
Whether coherentism can integrate logical, theological, and ethical commitments without an isolated foundational hierarchy.
Whether practical logical reliance includes a normative obligation to reason consistently and validly.
The decisive demand is whether repeated reliability can warrant logical reliance without an ultimate divine guarantee.
A further demand is why an integrated coherentist worldview requires God rather than allowing logical commitments to remain basic or mutually supported.
Whether permitting unexplained logical basics while demanding explanation of God constitutes an arbitrary stopping-point asymmetry.
Whether practical reliance without an external ontology licenses treating logical commitments as unexplained basics.
The decisive component is whether treating logic or metaphysical commitments as basic creates an arbitrary exemption that equally permits God as a stopping point.
Whether exposing an explanatory dead end or arbitrary stopping point establishes the alternative conclusion that God exists.
Whether a divine explanation follows before necessity is demonstrated and alternative explanations are excluded.
The decisive demand is whether exposing an arbitrary or unexplained stopping point positively establishes God as the necessary alternative.
A specifically divine conclusion requires excluding alternative explanations and establishing the necessity of an explanation in the first place.
Whether transcendental preconditions warrant a proof method distinct from ordinary empirical inference and ordinary explanatory elimination.
Whether denial of fundamental categories would undermine the possibility of argument, knowledge, and communication.
The decisive demand is what proof standard applies when denial of a paradigm-level precondition allegedly destroys argument, knowledge, and communication.
The move also bears on why fundamental preconditions might require a nonordinary justification rather than ordinary evidential comparison.
Whether induction can be rationally warranted as fallible inference rather than deductively proved or externally guaranteed.
Whether induction's nondeductive character makes it equivalent to unsupported guessing.
The decisive demand is whether induction can receive rational fallibilist warrant from observations without deductive certainty or theistic grounding.
The move also contests treating induction as requiring the same certainty or proof form as a deductive or transcendental principle.
Whether failure to provide ultimate justification makes the con worldview incoherent rather than merely incomplete or fallibilist.
Whether practical reliability can sustain epistemic coherence without an ultimate transcendental account.
Whether transcendental justification positively establishes God rather than only alleging collapse of a rival worldview.
The decisive demand is to demonstrate why fundamental commitments require a further ground and why God resolves rather than relocates that requirement.
A further demand is how alleged worldview incoherence yields a positive argument for God's existence rather than only criticism of an opponent.
Whether logical regularities require a divine mind or may persist as mind-independent descriptive features of reality.
Whether acknowledging descriptive logical regularities without a separate ontology makes a worldview incoherent.
The decisive demand is whether logical laws require ontology as prescriptive abstract entities grounded in a divine mind.
The reply also asks whether accepting mind-independent descriptive regularity is coherent despite inability to observe a mindless universe.
Whether criticism of the theistic warrant incurs a burden to prove God's nonexistence or provide a complete rival worldview.
Whether withholding acceptance of the pro reasons is equivalent to asserting an arbitrary opposite conclusion.
The decisive demand is whether skeptical criticism incurs a burden to prove the opposite conclusion or provide an entire rival worldview.
The attribution of arbitrariness also depends on treating withheld assent as a positive assertion rather than a challenge to the offered warrant.
Whether the transcendental case provides enough explicit inferential structure to test validity and soundness.
Whether labeling the proof transcendental removes the need to state premises and the bridge to the specifically theistic conclusion.
The decisive demand is for explicit premises and inferential structure sufficient to test whether the claimed worldview collapse validly supports God.
Calling the proof transcendental or distinct does not remove the need for assessable structure and sound premises.
Whether an obligation to reason consistently can be justified by shared practical aims without theistic grounding.
Whether practical and ethical normativity must rest on an invariant divine foundation.
The decisive demand is why one ought to reason consistently and whether that practical norm requires integration with God and theistic ethics.
The reply also addresses the normative role of logic within inquiry by appealing to reduced error and danger.
Whether the transcendental proof has an identifiable positive form: denial of a fundamental principle presupposes that principle.
Whether presupposition in denial supplies a positive proof rather than merely an explanatory dead end.
Whether this denial structure establishes the specifically Orthodox divine ground rather than only a general precondition.
The decisive demand is an explicit account of how a transcendental proof works and what inferential feature makes it positive rather than empirical.
The move also addresses why denial-based presupposition is intended to be positive proof rather than a mere explanatory dead end.
It purports to supply affirmative warrant by locating proof in what denial itself must assume.
Whether Orthodox theology identifies logical laws with God's essence or offers a more qualified relation through divine energies and actions.
Whether the essence-energies distinction independently demonstrates the existence or necessity of the divine guarantor.
The decisive demand is how Orthodox theology locates logical laws without treating them as external entities or direct descriptions of the divine essence.
